The Arctic Environmental Responsibility Index was created in 2021 by a group of multinational academics (Overland et al 2021). Oil and gas companies operating in the Arctic were evaluated on criteria of how they were minimizing harm to local ecosystems and Indigenous people near their operations (ibid). Out of all the Arctic countries, the companies that are headquartered in the American Empire average the highest ratings while the Russian Empire has the worst environmental ratings (ibid). Trends within the data showed that oil and gas companies have a better rating than mining, likely because mining is inland while oil is offshore (ibid). However,
the Arctic Environmental Responsibility Index lacks an analysis of scale.
The lowest-ranking company, based in Russia, has a mere 2 percent of the revenues of the highest-ranking company from Norway (“Rating of the Largest Russian Companies by Sales Volume” 2018).
While larger corporations score higher on the index, their environmental impact may be higher due to the sheer amount of resource extraction undergone.

It isn’t just marine Arctic ecosystems that are suffering. The evidence is in the soil. Soil acts as one of the world’s primary storage of carbon, keeping it away from the atmosphere and thereby mitigating climate change (Volkova 2021). Half of the global supply of soil organic carbon is in the Arctic (Thawing Arctic Peatlands Risk Unlocking Huge Amounts of Carbon” 2019). These 1.7 trillion tons of carbon in the Arctic predominantly come from peat, an organic soil that is made out of partially decomposed plant matter (“Histosols” 2024). Like sea ice, much of these soils remain frozen year-round, hence the name permafrost (Tvid et al 2012).
But as accelerating warming thaws this permafrost
As water moves through the deepest layers of the soil, the wet peat gets exposed to oxygen and

(Pearce 2017). The thawing of permafrost also awakens microbes deep in the ground, who find these warming temperatures ideal for growing (ibid). Like humans, microbes release greenhouse gasses as a byproduct of their daily respiration (Barbato et al 2022). And so more microbes means more greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere (ibid). However, not all microbes are reacting to climate change equally, leading to uneven microbe population distribution which threatens the microbial ecosystem and subsequently the health of the soil (Mallard & Pearce 2018). These effects are complicated by the soil ecosystem differences across the Arctic, all of which remain vastly under-researched (Barbato et al 2022).

A possible analysis from the Arctic Responsibility Index is that the blame for colonialism in the Arctic has shifted from the state to corporations, but out of the 120 companies listed on the index, 15 are state-owned (Overland et al 2021). The most environmentally responsible company is one of them. The Norwegian government has a 67% stake in this company named Equinor (“Our Shareholders”). In 2022 the oil corporation posted record profits, leaving the government with a payout of 11.390 billion dollars (“Equinor Fourth Quarter 2022 and Year End Results”).1 Another Norse state-owned oil company, Petoro is ranked number 33 (Overland et al 2021).
